lessons: Never repeat the hook or title question in the first sentence: repeating the prompt in videos like 'Potatoes Sprout' and 'Garlic' caused immediate drops of 31.9% and 34.0% at the 10% mark.

Cut filler transition lines that state the obvious: generic setup sentences like 'They look like similar fruits' ('Fruits Float') and 'They are not just there to look cool' ('Car Windshields') lost over 30% of viewers in the first seconds.
Avoid pause-and-guess prompts or countdowns: interrupting the narrative flow with 'Pause and guess... three, two, one' led to significant drop-offs (e.g., 15.2% drop at 37% in the Foil video).

Anchor hooks in extreme scale or surprising contrasts: videos comparing unexpected facts ('older than the United States', 'tuna is red meat, cod is white') achieved the highest end retention (45% to 108%).
Use direct second-person roleplay to frame explanations: immersive scenarios ('You're a baby tyrannosaur') held viewer retention well above channel average throughout the video.
worst_moment_types: Immediate repetition or rephrasing of the video's hook line
Generic filler lines stating common knowledge or obvious facts
Interactive friction points like 'Pause and guess' prompts or countdowns
Dense technical jargon introduced before establishing the main payoff
best_hook_types: Bold comparison anchored in historical or physical scale ('older than the United States')
Striking visual paradox or contrast ('tuna meat is red, cod is white')
Intriguing secret or paradigm shift ('Most James Webb images hold secrets', solar system edge extension)
Direct second-person scenario framing ('You're a baby tyrannosaur...')
